questions.prompt: What rule does Chapter 6 give for assigning disruptive responsibility?
choices: Put the effort with the organization whose customers need the disruptive technology
Always keep the effort in the largest incumbent unit
Move every disruptive project into an outside company immediately

explanation.gentle: The chapter says responsibility should follow customer need.
explanation.direct: Customer-fit placement is the chapter's central rule.
explanation.competitive: Send the work where demand is alive.

questions.prompt: Why does customer pull matter so much in this chapter?
choices: Because customer demand shapes what an organization seriously prioritizes
Because executive speeches stop mattering completely
Because disruptive technologies have no technical challenges

explanation.gentle: Organizations keep following the customers that define their success.
explanation.direct: Budgets and attention bend toward the demand system the unit already serves.
explanation.competitive: The paying audience writes the urgency list.

questions.prompt: Why can the wrong organizational home damage a disruptive effort?
choices: Because the unit may rationally keep serving different customers instead
Because all incumbent units are badly managed
Because structure never matters in innovation

explanation.gentle: The unit can neglect the effort simply because its customers do not need it enough.
explanation.direct: Wrong-home ownership creates rational neglect, not necessarily open sabotage.
explanation.competitive: The project gets starved by a smart unit serving the wrong people.

questions.prompt: Elena's pilot sits in the premium unit, but that unit's customers do not want the disruptive offering. What best fits Chapter 6?
choices: Keep the project there because the premium unit has the most prestige
Move responsibility toward the group whose customers would actually need the offering
Cancel the effort because it lacks mainstream pull

explanation.gentle: Ownership should go where customer need gives the effort a real reason to matter.
explanation.direct: The chapter says placement should follow live demand, not incumbent status.
explanation.competitive: Stop letting the wrong customers run the case.

questions.prompt: What does Chapter 6 say about executive support?
choices: It solves the ownership problem by itself
It matters, but it cannot fully override the priorities created by the unit's customer base
It should be ignored whenever a project is disruptive

explanation.gentle: Leaders can support the project, but the unit still follows the customers that justify its work.
explanation.direct: Executive intention has limits when customer pull keeps shaping the organization's priorities.
explanation.competitive: A blessing from above does not silence the live queue.

questions.prompt: What is a misreading of Chapter 6?
choices: Every disruptive effort must become a fully separate company immediately
The wrong home can create rational neglect
Autonomy matters when it changes which customers define success

explanation.gentle: The chapter's rule is narrower than that. It is about customer-fit placement.
explanation.direct: Chapter 6 does not turn separation into a universal command.
explanation.competitive: This is not spin-off theater for everything.

questions.prompt: In a school workshop, a beginner tool is owned by the advanced elective team even though beginners use it daily. What should the class reconsider?
choices: Whether ownership should follow the group whose users actually need the tool
Whether beginners should stop using the tool
Whether advanced students should be banned from tool decisions

explanation.gentle: The right home is decided by need, not status alone.
explanation.direct: Chapter 6 asks who the real customer is before deciding who should own the work.
explanation.competitive: Let demand, not prestige, choose the judges.

questions.prompt: Why does Priya's side project keep getting buried in the main backlog?
choices: Because the established unit's customers barely notice it, so other work keeps scoring higher
Because side projects never matter strategically
Because smaller groups are always less competent

explanation.gentle: The owning unit keeps serving the customers who matter most to it right now.
explanation.direct: The project stalls because it sits inside the wrong customer logic.
explanation.competitive: The queue keeps voting for other work.

questions.prompt: Why is Chapter 6 more unsettling than a simple call to 'support innovation'?
choices: Because it shows that a competent organization can still starve a disruptive effort when the wrong customers define success
Because it argues that customers never matter
Because it says organization charts are the only thing that matters

explanation.gentle: The problem is deeper than attitude. The wrong home can produce neglect even with capable managers.
explanation.direct: Rational underinvestment can emerge from structural customer misfit rather than obvious resistance.
explanation.competitive: Good process can still suffocate the future if the wrong demand system rules.

questions.prompt: If Chapter 6 fixes the ownership problem, what question does Chapter 7 naturally open next?
choices: Whether the owning organization is the right size for the market it serves
Whether customers should be ignored after ownership changes
Whether every future chapter can now skip organizational design

explanation.gentle: Once the effort has the right home, managers still have to ask whether that home can live on the market's scale.
explanation.direct: The next issue is market-size fit, not ownership alone.
explanation.competitive: After the right address comes the scale test.
